It's allowed me to ship 2,000 PRs a month to production with high confidence. Personally, I have never put much emphasis into how many lines of code or how many PRs I was landing. Before agents, no one cared, and rightfully so, as raw productivity did not always equate to quality or a visible outcome for users. It was simply a vanity metric. But I've discovered through the course of building pstack that volume does matter, especially when you are able to maintain or even increase the level of quality of the product with agents. For example, I started working on Grok @Bot about 2 months ago, when it was still in its early days and the codebase was fresh but starting to grow. Despite the team growing and now landing hundreds of PRs a day into the Grok @Bot codebase, pstack has allowed me to keep the quality of the code high for everyone as I constantly monitor code, refactor, add new lints and checks, and also work on features. Being Grok @Bot's gardener and maintainer is something I was only able to do through pstack. Our early momentum after building the prototype was very high and many people were joining the team. I had a critical moment of opportunity to refactor the whole codebase, while it was being built and extended and with no downtime, into something with strong foundations. A codebase with high quality that scales no matter how many engineers (and most importantly, non-engineers) contribute to it. All of this work requires me to refactor and improve the foundations of Grok Bot as it's being built, and you can only do that when the foundations can keep up with the number of contributions. The proof is in Grok @Bot itself. Over the next few weeks, I'll tell you everything you need to know to be able to build and maintain a high quality app using pstack. # Part 1 – Verification is all you need The most critical skill to have in your toolbox is a high quality verification skill. This skill is so important to have and maintain that I think of it more like critical infrastructure rather than "just" a skill. A good one will amplify the output of your whole team, including non-engineers. Done well, you will 100-1000x your whole team's output. If you're not familiar with the term, verification means that an agent can verify its own work. It can keep going until it succeeds at its task, because it can now close the loop without you being the bottleneck. If you're interested to know more of the story of how I created my first verification skill for Cursor, check out my previous post Loops You Can Trust. ## Let's build a verification skill together To start, install pstack and then run `/create-verification-skill`. I also recommend adding Dr Eggbot, my bot that helps you create high quality bots, to your roster. Dr Eggbot ships with pstack. It’ll teach coding bots how to use it, and it can also make non-coding bots with the same rigor. You can ask Dr Eggbot to create an engineer bot for you that you can then ask to run `/create-verification-skill` and set up a daily routine to run `/maintain-verification-skill`. While that runs, let's walk through what the skill does and how it makes a high quality verification skill for you. I distilled all of our verification skills that we use to build Grok @Bot and Cursor into this skill as a sort of meta-skill. It teaches your agent how to create a high quality one for your own app. Now this is where choice of tech stack is important. If you're building an app in Electron or for the web for example, you can take advantage of the rich debugging tools available for the JS ecosystem. For example, the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) allows you to use the same tooling available in your browser's developer tools. Or if you're building an iOS app, making use of the simulator. input.title: X articles reach the recipe without their images: firecrawl serves a text-only rendition
input.description:
An X article loses its inline screenshots and images before extraction starts. Firecrawl does not return x.com's page: it serves its own rendition of the post, and that rendition carries no images, so no recipe can recover them. Observed on 2026-10-04 by scraping [https://x.com/poteto/status/2094457600259842065]() (Lauren Tan's post about pstack) with the same call `FirecrawlFetcher` makes (`formats=["rawHtml", "markdown"]`, `proxy="auto"`): * `rawHtml` is a 19 KB synthesized document, not x.com's markup. It opens with `

Post by @poteto

` and a paragraph carrying `Author:`, `Posted:`, `URL:` and `Likes: … | Retweets: …`, then an `

Post

` and the post body as plain HTML. * The body keeps its structure: 5 `
`, 3 `
`, 3 lists, the headings, and inline ``. The original report that code, lists and quotes were flattened came from the retired trafilatura path and no longer holds.
* There is no `` anywhere in `rawHtml` and no image in `markdown`.
* The scrape billed **30 credits** on a basic proxy, against 1 to 5 for an ordinary page.

Open decisions:

* How to get X's images: a different fetch for x.com behind the `Fetcher` interface (`api/app/service/fetch.py`), a firecrawl option that keeps media, or X's own API or syndication endpoints.
* Whether X articles are worth 30 credits each, independent of the image question.
* Whether the synthesized header (author, date, likes) is something the x.com recipe must ignore, or something a different fetch removes.

Keep the URL as a regression fixture for whichever fetch replaces this one. See `docs/technical-design/article-extraction.md` ("Fetching the page") and `docs/technical-design/recipes.md`.

input.description:
Extraction that can be trusted and extended per site. A generic base extraction plus declarative per-domain recipes (substack, medium and similar behave the same once described), an agent loop that writes a recipe for an unknown site, auto-validation gates that fail an item whose extraction is not the article before anyone has to report it, and a per-recipe fetch strategy (direct fetch with a browser user agent, firecrawl, or a real browser) with firecrawl kept as a pluggable backend.

Build order: validation gates, then recipe schema and resolver, then the agent recipe loop, then fetch pluggability, then a reporting UI only if still needed. Paywalled credentials are deferred, possibly forever.

This replaces an earlier plan that put an LLM in the extraction hot path (firecrawl always, HTML always, an LLM instead of trafilatura, with a prompt eval system). The recipes approach keeps per-request extraction deterministic and moves the intelligence to authoring time.

**Closed on 2026-10-04.** What shipped: the recipe runtime that runs a stored script deterministically (ASE-6), the Flue authoring and revision agents (ASE-7), the extraction service on Cloudflare (ASE-61) and the API's integration with it (ASE-63); trafilatura is retired. What was dropped: the validation gates (ASE-5, ASE-24), replaced by the validator plus the agents' not-an-article verdict, and the per-recipe fetch strategy (ASE-8), firecrawl staying the one fetch behind the `Fetcher` interface. The defects found afterwards on real articles moved to the Extraction issues milestone; the trafilatura-era bugs that recipes made moot (ASE-25, ASE-26) were canceled. The reporting UI (ASE-9) moved out with the web surfaces.

input.name: Web app
input.description:
The logged-in web surface around the read-along player: the listener's list of items, their settings, the ways out of the player to the original article, a way to report a bad extraction, and serving the web frontend and the API from one origin. The player itself is the Read-along player milestone, its look is Read-along visual design, and the public funnel (landing page, login, first item) is Validate demand.

To be shaped and designed before tasks are written; the issues gathered here are candidates carried over from the backlog, not a settled scope.

{"id":"ASE-18","uuid":"d8b28c73-42b6-44dc-b497-e9b9eba19f70","title":"Serve the web frontend and the API from one origin","description":"Design decision: serve the web frontend and the API from one origin (for example `nagara.asermax.com`) instead of separate hosts. Same-origin removes CORS, simplifies the cookie/session story for the future player's authentication, and gives a clean presigned-audio flow.

The constraint: Railway maps a domain to one service, so one surface must own the domain and route to the other over private networking. The question to settle is which surface owns the domain and proxies to the other.

Options:

* Preferred: the TanStack Start server owns the domain and proxies `/api/*` to the API service over `nagara-api.railway.internal:8080`.
* A dedicated reverse-proxy service.
* A Cloudflare Worker doing path routing.

Timing: do this when the web frontend lands, not before. It is one session of comparison once there is a `web/` tree to route to. Read `docs/technical-design/deployment-and-ci.md` before touching deploy configuration (two dashboard-only Railway settings matter and are not in `railway.toml`) and `docs/technical-design/authentication.md` for the current auth model. The two deployables ship independently and neither pipeline reaches into the other's tree (`docs/technical-design/invariants.md`).","projectMilestone":{"id":"18988974-aac9-429e-b371-b77e185af3f4","name":"Web app"},"priority":{"value":3,"name":"Medium"},"url":"https://linear.app/asermax/issue/ASE-18/serve-the-web-frontend-and-the-api-from-one-origin","gitBranchName":"asermax/ase-18-serve-the-web-frontend-and-the-api-from-one-origin","createdAt":"2026-09-07T03:37:46.774Z","updatedAt":"2026-10-05T00:37:43.011Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Improvement"],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Agustin Carrasco","createdById":"c8b03f1c-0b66-413e-85b8-f11067346ca8","project":"nagara","projectId":"14d108e2-6712-4129-b37d-e021d5aa2f0b","team":"Asermax","teamId":"c821b24b-23d9-403e-9038-23d9024a2110"}

content.text:
Extraction v2 is closed: it has no open issues left, so it shows as 100%. Its description now ends with a note on what shipped and what was dropped.

**ASE-10 (X articles):** you were right, it's the fetch. When I scraped the poteto post through firecrawl with the same call the API makes, it returned firecrawl's own 19 KB rendition of the post instead of x.com's page. That rendition keeps the code blocks, quotes, lists and headings but contains no images at all, and it adds a header with author, date and likes. The scrape cost **30 credits**, where a normal page costs 1 to 5. I rewrote the issue around these findings, with the open decisions: a different fetch for x.com, or whether X is worth 30 credits per article. It's in Extraction issues now.

**Linear changes:**
- **ASE-25 and ASE-26**: canceled, each with a comment explaining why recipes make it moot.
- **Extraction issues** (new milestone): holds ASE-10 and ASE-27. In ASE-27 I fixed the function name and the description of how footnote markers are excluded today.
- **Web app** (new milestone): holds ASE-9, plus the loose web tasks ASE-15 (article list), ASE-16 (settings), ASE-17 (link to the original article) and ASE-18 (one origin). Its description says the scope still needs shaping.

ASE-18 matters for the Cloudflare migration. Its options assume Railway, including the TanStack server proxying to `nagara-api.railway.internal`, and that question may change depending on what moves to Cloudflare.

# Nagara — audio article queue

**Status (2026-09-07):** Deployed and in daily use — powers the listen pipeline on tachikoma-pages (TTS + paragraph sync + images). The backlog now lives in **Linear** (workspace asermax, project nagara), and the repo's docs follow mahou's charter and template; the repo's quest log is gone. Current work: the **Extraction v2** milestone — per-domain recipes, agent-written recipes for unknown sites, auto-validation gates to catch silent bad extractions, and the lossy X-post fix. The original sketch is archived at [[04_Archive/2026-09-05-nagara-extraction-v2|extraction v2 note]]; the milestone is the live plan.

**Name: Nagara (ながら)** — from *ながら聞き*, consuming content while doing something else.

Related: [[03_Resources/software-engineering/hegel-bend2-verified-specs]] — parked research on Hegel (property tests for the sync/extraction invariants) and Bend 2 (laws as verifiable specs for the extraction pipeline).

## Repo state (synced 2026-09-07)

Repo: `~/workspace/asermax/nagara`, on `main` at `d321a1c` (2026-09-07). Production at `nagara.asermax.com` (Railway, scale-to-zero, Postgres + S3 bucket) with the TTS service on Modal; `/health` answers. CI runs test/lint/types per subproject; `tts/` auto-deploys from CI, `api/` from Railway's GitHub integration. The repo's `docs/` holds `technical-design/` (how the code works) and `product-design/` (what nagara is) under mahou's charter, with hand-kept indexes and relative links; that is where the detail lives. Work in flight is never in `docs/`.

**Built:** the API spine (enqueue → extract → spawn TTS → poll → audio), single API-key auth on every route, Alembic migrations, a step-based item pipeline with per-step persistence, markdown-formatted paragraphs, article images stored as image units and described with Gemini, code blocks described, a cost ledger per Firecrawl/TTS/describer call, footnote-marker pruning, XML-tagged-word and empty-element extraction fixes. The read-along player runs on tachikoma-pages, not in the repo's `web/`, which is still empty on `main`.

**Not built:** `web/`, Google OAuth, quota, settings, landing, article list. The [[mvp]] spec describes the original plan; the agreed build order is dogfood first (API hardening → article list → settings), then the public funnel (auth → article creation → landing), each in service of validating demand.

**Backlog in Linear (2026-09-07):** 40 issues on the nagara project, five milestones. **Extraction v2** (ASE-5 to ASE-10, ASE-24 to ASE-27): validation gates, recipe schema and resolver, agent recipe loop, per-recipe fetch strategy, reporting UI if still needed, the X-post bug, plus the trustworthy-extraction research, unfenced-code-as-prose, prose boilerplate and literal footnote markers. **Validate demand** (ASE-11 to ASE-13): OAuth login, web article creation, landing. **Formulas read aloud** (ASE-36 done, ASE-37 to ASE-39): MathML recovery, described display formulas, raw delimiters. **Read-along player** (ASE-40 done, ASE-41 to ASE-43): the surface, image unit rendering, playback speed. **Read-along visual design** (ASE-44). Loose: API hardening (ASE-14), article list, settings, link-and-share, single origin, describe-budget starvation, quote voice switching, audio caching, caption export, bookmarklet, three test gaps, the audible-markdown criterion, and four open questions (castable video, streaming paragraph audio, markdown faithfulness, pricing model). In Todo: ASE-5, ASE-10, ASE-24.

**Conventions:** branches are `feat/<feature-name>`; a feature is shaped and designed (mahou:shape, mahou:design) and its design lands as a note before a milestone gets implementation tasks; a spike is throwaway and never merges. The earlier LLM-in-the-hot-path extraction plan is superseded by the recipes approach and no longer exists as a record. Only `idea/read-along-player` remains as a non-main branch, kept on purpose as the player shape spike.

Turn [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]]'s existing audio-article generation into a standalone product. The pipeline already exists — chunking, TTS voice selection, audio stitching — so the bet is that the hard technical part is done and the open question is demand and packaging.

**MVP is defined** — see [[mvp]] for the full spec (surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market).

## The Idea

**Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A private personal audio read-later queue, API-first: enqueue an article (web paste or agent push) → it's generated into read-along audio → listen from your queue when it suits you. The web paste-and-listen page is the front door; the queue-for-later is the real objective, and a solid API lets [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] push reading-list items straight into it.

## Why

The pipeline is already built and working inside Tachikoma. Productizing it is mostly a matter of wrapping a demand-validation surface around code that already runs, rather than inventing the core capability.

## MVP

Full spec in [[mvp]]. In short: a private audio read-later queue with Google login, an eager `enqueue(url, voice?)` primitive shared by web and API, a 5-item/month free quota, all Kokoro voices (plus Random) with a per-user default, and an API key so Tachikoma can push items. Publicly fetchable articles only; uploads and paywalled content deferred.

## Technical Research (2026-07-10)

Ran a hands-on experiment on **Kokoro-82M** (open-weight TTS) + serverless GPU hosting. Full details in [[research]]; general reference in [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] and [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]]. Key results for this product:

- **Latency is a solved problem.** A 20-min article synthesizes in ~38 s on Replicate's T4 (zero-effort) or ~21 s on a Modal L4 — well inside a "don't leave the user waiting" budget. No exotic infra needed.
- **The pricing/token-cost open question now has real numbers:** ~**$0.008 per 20-min article** on Replicate (bills active compute only), or ~$0.004–0.005 batched on Modal. At 2,000 articles/mo that's single-digit dollars — TTS compute is **not** the cost risk it was assumed to be. A per-audio-minute usage model comfortably covers it.
- **Hosting decision: going with Modal** (Kokoro on L4 + memory snapshotting). Owned endpoint, ~6 s cold start, ~$0 at expected volume — and crucially it lets us return **timing metadata** alongside the audio, which the read-along feature needs. Design + code in [[modal-tts-service]]. (Replicate's public model was the quick validation path but doesn't return timings.)
- **Read-along is a core feature, not a bonus:** the page highlights the paragraph currently being read, synced to audio. Achieved by synthesizing paragraph-by-paragraph and tracking cumulative time for exact paragraph ranges; Kokoro's free per-word timestamps (English) are also captured for future word-level highlighting. See [[modal-tts-service]].

## Open Questions

- ~~**Pricing vs. token cost.**~~ **Largely answered** — compute is ~$0.008/20-min article; a per-audio-minute or metered-tier model works. Remaining nuance: bundling vs. metering for UX.
- **File uploads.** Handling user-provided content (PDFs, docs) is a whole surface of its own — deferred past MVP.
- **Paywalled articles.** Fetching content behind paywalls is both a technical and a legal/ethical question — deferred.
- **Is there an audience?** The entire point of starting tiny is to find out before investing. **This is now the main gate** — the tech and cost are de-risked. Validation plan (dogfood via Tachikoma, Show HN / communities, read-later + accessibility crowds) in [[mvp]]; SEO is deliberately *not* the first channel.

## Connections

- [[mvp]] — full MVP spec: surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market
- [[modal-tts-service]] — chosen hosting design + timing/highlighting approach + code
- [[research]] — TTS engine + hosting experiment, benchmarks, cost analysis
- [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] — model capabilities reference
- [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]] — hosting/cost reference
- [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] — source of the existing audio pipeline
- [[02_Areas/Daily_Notes/2026-07-05]] — original capture

# Nagara — MVP definition

> **Note (2026-09-06):** this is the original MVP spec from July. The repo's agreed build order and what has actually shipped are summarised in [[index#Repo state (synced 2026-09-06)|the project index]]; the web surfaces, Google login and quota below are not built yet.

**Name: Nagara (ながら)** — from *ながら聞き* (nagara-giki), consuming content *while doing something else*. It names the benefit, not the mechanism, and is short/brandable with no baggage.

**Positioning: Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A **private** personal audio read-later queue, API-first. Your queue is yours; nothing is publicly shared by default. This posture is deliberate — see [Go-to-market](#go-to-market) — it keeps traffic on the original articles, dodges the copyright problem of mirroring content, and makes distribution about the *tool*, not other people's content.

## Core primitive

Both the web and the API are clients of one operation:

`enqueue(url, voice?) → generate eagerly → private item in your queue with a listen link`

Generation is **eager**: when an item lands (web paste or agent push), audio synthesis starts immediately, so by the time you open your queue everything is ready. Items carry a status: `queued → generating → ready`.

## Web surfaces (5 pages)

1. **Landing** — paste a public article URL (the demo hook). Stashes the URL → sends you to Google login → replays it as your first queued item after auth. The pasted URL must survive the OAuth redirect (stash + replay) so the funnel stays seamless.
2. **Google login** — OAuth, resolves to a user.
3. **Queue** — your list of items with status and a link to each item's player. Home base.
4. **Read-along player** — audio + paragraph highlighting + click-to-seek (design in [[modal-tts-service]]). **Private** (behind login), not a public share link. The wow moment.
5. **Settings** — default voice (all Kokoro voices + **Random**) and **API key management** (create/revoke).

## API (the real workflow — Tachikoma pushes here)

The queue-for-later is the actual objective; the web paste-and-listen is the friendly front door into it. The API is what [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] calls to push reading-list items.

- `POST /items` — `{url, voice?}`, auth via **API key** *or* session → enqueues, starts eager generation, returns the item + listen link. The one the agent calls.
- `GET /items` — list your queue.
- `GET /items/:id` — status + audio URL + timing JSON.
- **API keys act as the user** — pushes land in that user's queue and count against that user's quota. One key per user is enough for now.

## Quota — tiers (same mechanism, per-user number)

- **Free: 5 items / month.**
- **Owner (me): high / unlimited** — seeded high so my own Tachikoma pushes aren't capped during the MVP.
- **Paid: later** — a paying-customer tier comes after validation. For now the limit just hard-blocks with a "more coming" message.

Quota **counts items enqueued, not compute** — cleaner mental model ("your list this month"). Eager generation counts against the limit when you have one.

## Voice

- Per-user **default voice**, changeable on the settings page. All Kokoro voices available.
- **Random** is an option — picks a random voice from the set. Random **resolves to a concrete voice at generation time and is stored on the item**, so re-listens and the highlight timing stay stable.
- API push uses the user's default voice unless `voice` is passed explicitly (the agent won't pick one interactively).

## Explicitly out of scope (MVP)

- Payment / upgrade flow (quota just hard-blocks for now).
- File uploads (PDFs/docs), paywalled content.
- Word-level highlighting (paragraph-level only; word timestamps captured for later — see [[modal-tts-service]]).
- Audio caching by `(url, voice)` — nice optimization, deliberately skipped for now.
- Public share links, browser extension / bookmarklet.
- Decay-based queue cleanup, multiple API keys per user.

## Go-to-market

**SEO is the wrong first move.** It compounds over months, needs content/authority we don't have, and answers "can I scale traffic?" — not the MVP question, "does anyone want this?" We can answer demand with zero SEO.

Because Nagara is a **private tool, not a content platform**, distribution is about the tool, never about leaking anyone's article. Channels, per priority:

- **Dogfood via Tachikoma (definitely).** I'm user zero — if it fixes my own reading-list guilt, that's the strongest signal and gives authentic things to say.
- **Show HN + communities (maybe).** Pitch *the tool* ("I built an audio read-later queue"). One good post can bring a burst of real users to validate demand.
- **Read-later + accessibility communities (maybe).** The Pocket/Instapaper/Readwise crowd already has the habit; dyslexia / ADHD / low-vision / language-learner communities have a real need. Concrete, reachable audiences.
- **Dropped for now:** "Save to Nagara" bookmarklet / browser extension. Good acquisition + capture surface, but deferred past this MVP.

Copyright note for the future: any *public* pages hosting audio of others' articles carry copyright nuance — the private-tool posture sidesteps it entirely for now.

## Connections

- [[index]] — the idea overview
- [[modal-tts-service]] — TTS service design, response shape, read-along player, audio format
- [[research]] — engine + hosting experiment, benchmarks, cost analysis
- [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] — source of the pipeline and the agent that will push items via the API

# TTS engine & hosting research

Hands-on experiment (2026-07-10) to de-risk the technical side of [[index|the audio-article product]]: which TTS engine, how to host it on-demand, does it hit a "fast enough" bar, and what does it actually cost per article. General reusable knowledge lives in [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] and [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]] — this note is the product-specific decision trail.

## Requirement we designed against

- **Async is fine, but fast** — "don't leave users waiting." Target: a **20-minute article rendered in ≤60 s**.
- **Bursty / on-demand** — generate when an article is requested/published, pay ~zero when idle.
- Translates to: **≥20× real-time sustained**, with cold-start time spent from the same budget.

## Engine: Kokoro-82M

Picked Kokoro (open-weight, 82M params, <2 GB VRAM, near-human quality). Findings that matter here:

- **GPU: ~40–160× real-time** depending on card → a 20-min article is seconds of compute. Latency target is trivially met on any real GPU.
- **CPU: only ~2.9× real-time** → ~7 min for a 20-min article. Rules out CPU-only hosting for this latency bar without ~7× chunk-parallelism.
- **Free per-word timestamps** (English) — enables read-along highlighting / synced captions with no extra alignment step. Potential product differentiator.

# Nagara — MVP definition

> **Note (2026-09-06):** this is the original MVP spec from July. The repo's agreed build order and what has actually shipped are summarised in [[index#Repo state (synced 2026-09-06)|the project index]]; the web surfaces, Google login and quota below are not built yet.

**Name: Nagara (ながら)** — from *ながら聞き* (nagara-giki), consuming content *while doing something else*. It names the benefit, not the mechanism, and is short/brandable with no baggage.

**Positioning: Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A **private** personal audio read-later queue, API-first. Your queue is yours; nothing is publicly shared by default. This posture is deliberate — see [Go-to-market](#go-to-market) — it keeps traffic on the original articles, dodges the copyright problem of mirroring content, and makes distribution about the *tool*, not other people's content.

## Core primitive

Both the web and the API are clients of one operation:

`enqueue(url, voice?) → generate eagerly → private item in your queue with a listen link`

Generation is **eager**: when an item lands (web paste or agent push), audio synthesis starts immediately, so by the time you open your queue everything is ready. Items carry a status: `queued → generating → ready`.

## Web surfaces (5 pages)

1. **Landing** — paste a public article URL (the demo hook). Stashes the URL → sends you to Google login → replays it as your first queued item after auth. The pasted URL must survive the OAuth redirect (stash + replay) so the funnel stays seamless.
2. **Google login** — OAuth, resolves to a user.
3. **Queue** — your list of items with status and a link to each item's player. Home base.
4. **Read-along player** — audio + paragraph highlighting + click-to-seek (design in [[modal-tts-service]]). **Private** (behind login), not a public share link. The wow moment.
5. **Settings** — default voice (all Kokoro voices + **Random**) and **API key management** (create/revoke).

## API (the real workflow — Tachikoma pushes here)

The queue-for-later is the actual objective; the web paste-and-listen is the friendly front door into it. The API is what [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] calls to push reading-list items.

- `POST /items` — `{url, voice?}`, auth via **API key** *or* session → enqueues, starts eager generation, returns the item + listen link. The one the agent calls.
- `GET /items` — list your queue.
- `GET /items/:id` — status + audio URL + timing JSON.
- **API keys act as the user** — pushes land in that user's queue and count against that user's quota. One key per user is enough for now.

## Quota — tiers (same mechanism, per-user number)

- **Free: 5 items / month.**
- **Owner (me): high / unlimited** — seeded high so my own Tachikoma pushes aren't capped during the MVP.
- **Paid: later** — a paying-customer tier comes after validation. For now the limit just hard-blocks with a "more coming" message.

Quota **counts items enqueued, not compute** — cleaner mental model ("your list this month"). Eager generation counts against the limit when you have one.

## Voice

- Per-user **default voice**, changeable on the settings page. All Kokoro voices available.
- **Random** is an option — picks a random voice from the set. Random **resolves to a concrete voice at generation time and is stored on the item**, so re-listens and the highlight timing stay stable.
- API push uses the user's default voice unless `voice` is passed explicitly (the agent won't pick one interactively).

## Explicitly out of scope (MVP)

- Payment / upgrade flow (quota just hard-blocks for now).
- File uploads (PDFs/docs), paywalled content.
- Word-level highlighting (paragraph-level only; word timestamps captured for later — see [[modal-tts-service]]).
- Audio caching by `(url, voice)` — nice optimization, deliberately skipped for now.
- Public share links, browser extension / bookmarklet.
- Decay-based queue cleanup, multiple API keys per user.

## Go-to-market

**SEO is the wrong first move.** It compounds over months, needs content/authority we don't have, and answers "can I scale traffic?" — not the MVP question, "does anyone want this?" We can answer demand with zero SEO.

Because Nagara is a **private tool, not a content platform**, distribution is about the tool, never about leaking anyone's article. Channels, per priority:

- **Dogfood via Tachikoma (definitely).** I'm user zero — if it fixes my own reading-list guilt, that's the strongest signal and gives authentic things to say.
- **Show HN + communities (maybe).** Pitch *the tool* ("I built an audio read-later queue"). One good post can bring a burst of real users to validate demand.
- **Read-later + accessibility communities (maybe).** The Pocket/Instapaper/Readwise crowd already has the habit; dyslexia / ADHD / low-vision / language-learner communities have a real need. Concrete, reachable audiences.
- **Dropped for now:** "Save to Nagara" bookmarklet / browser extension. Good acquisition + capture surface, but deferred past this MVP.

Copyright note for the future: any *public* pages hosting audio of others' articles carry copyright nuance — the private-tool posture sidesteps it entirely for now.

- [[modal-tts-service]] — TTS service design, response shape, read-along player, audio format
- [[research]] — engine + hosting experiment, benchmarks, cost analysis
- [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] — source of the pipeline and the agent that will push items via the API

16-
17:Found it refreshing to see a product team building a thoughtful evolution pipeline instead of tearing everything down on the premise that AI now does everything. Resonates with his own labs-style setup (nagara, tachikoma) evolving alongside core work rather than replacing it.
##### 00_Inbox/gondolin-sandboxing-for-tachikoma.md
27-## Why it caught my attention
28-
29:[[tachikoma]] runs the Claude SDK with real credentials against real surfaces — Telegram, the vault, the Nagara API, deploys to tachikoma-pages. The egress policy and placeholder-token secret injection are the two pieces that map directly: the agent gets to use a credential without ever holding it, and its network reach becomes something declared rather than assumed.
30-
31-## Open questions before testing
32-
33-- Does an agent loop survive inside a micro-VM comfortably, or does the boot/snapshot cost make per-task VMs impractical for a always-on assistant?
34-- Tachikoma needs the vault on disk and git push access. Is that a VFS mount plus an egress allowlist, or does it fight the isolation model?
35-- Is the value here isolation for *my own* agent, or is this really infrastructure for running *untrusted* code — a different problem than the one I have?

11-# Hegel & Bend 2 — verified-spec tooling research
12-
13:Research from the Sep 27 tool-experiments capture (try Hegel, Bend, Lean). **Parked 2026-10-04: interesting, not being explored right now.** Connects to [[architecture-conformance-framework/index|Architecture Conformance Framework]] and [[01_Projects/nagara/index|Nagara]].
14-
15-Related: [[03_Resources/software-engineering/machine-checkable-architecture-specs]] (prior-art + design study), [[03_Resources/software-engineering/architecture-fitness-functions]].
16-
17-## Hegel — universal property-based testing (hegel.dev)
18-
19-Hypothesis's engine extracted into a Rust core (`libhegel`) with thin language frontends: TypeScript, Rust, Go, C++, Java, OCaml (Python uses Hypothesis itself — same engine).
20-
21-**How it works:** the frontend asks `libhegel` for a test case; the test body calls `tc.draw(generator)` per input, routing back into the core's generation/shrinking; the outcome is reported as valid / interesting (failure) / invalid / overran. On failure the core shrinks to a minimal counterexample and stores it in a database so reruns fail fast. Internal shrinking + replay DB are the Hypothesis advantages every language inherits.
22-
23-**Status:** developer preview; core is solid (it's Hypothesis), frontends rough. Official agent skill (`hegeldev/hegel-skill`) for agents writing property tests.
24-
25:**Fit for us:** invariant-shaped code — reading-list CLI state transitions, Nagara sync invariants (chunk count == timestamp count, monotonic unit indices), wallet reconciliation math, plan parser losslessness. Python CLIs can use Hypothesis directly today; Hegel earns its spot for TS/Rust/Go properties.
26-
27-## Bend 2 — programs with proofs built in (bend2.dev)
28-
29-Statically typed functional language: dependent types + machine-checked proofs + parallel execution (CPU via BendRT, GPU via `f!(x)` — Metal/CUDA). v2.0.32, active; Apache 2.0. Incompatible with Bend 1/HVM.
30-
31-**Answers the "actual program or simulation?" question:** laws and proofs live in the same `.bend` file as executable code; the compiler checks proofs before running; the native compiler emits C (proofs erased at runtime — zero cost). There is no separate simulation layer.
32-
33-```text
34-law round_trip:
35-  for command: Command
--
54-**Known gap:** the model–implementation gap is covered by statistical tests, not proofs. That matches the standing conclusion that conformance ≠ correctness and ROI lives at the spec level — Bend makes the spec side airtight.
55-
56:**Right-sized first experiments (parked):** Nagara sync invariants as laws + property tests; or the reading-list state machine. Both have provable cores and easy property-test translation. Alternative comparator: Lean + Aeneas (heavier ecosystem, tactics, verification of existing Rust).
57-
58-## Lean 4 (for completeness)
59-
60-Solid and production-relevant (SymCrypt, Linux kernel Rust verification via Aeneas). 2025–26 pattern: LLM writes proofs/specs, the Lean kernel certifies them. Demoted in favor of Bend 2 for our use — Bend covers the proof-carrying itch with lighter syntax; Lean wins only if we want the heavyweight ecosystem. "Hegel" the JS type checker (JSMonk) is unrelated and dormant — not the tool we meant.
#####
20:1. **Start every session**: Run `git pull` to sync latest changes
84:- **vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering** - 6-week FaMAF extension course, not yet scheduled; mirrors `filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`

# Nagara — audio article queue

**Status (2026-09-07):** Deployed and in daily use — powers the listen pipeline on tachikoma-pages (TTS + paragraph sync + images). The backlog now lives in **Linear** (workspace asermax, project nagara), and the repo's docs follow mahou's charter and template; the repo's quest log is gone. Current work: the **Extraction v2** milestone — per-domain recipes, agent-written recipes for unknown sites, auto-validation gates to catch silent bad extractions, and the lossy X-post fix. The original sketch is archived at [[04_Archive/2026-09-05-nagara-extraction-v2|extraction v2 note]]; the milestone is the live plan.

**Name: Nagara (ながら)** — from *ながら聞き*, consuming content while doing something else.

Related: [[03_Resources/software-engineering/hegel-bend2-verified-specs]] — parked research on Hegel (property tests for the sync/extraction invariants) and Bend 2 (laws as verifiable specs for the extraction pipeline).

## Repo state (synced 2026-09-07)

Repo: `~/workspace/asermax/nagara`, on `main` at `d321a1c` (2026-09-07). Production at `nagara.asermax.com` (Railway, scale-to-zero, Postgres + S3 bucket) with the TTS service on Modal; `/health` answers. CI runs test/lint/types per subproject; `tts/` auto-deploys from CI, `api/` from Railway's GitHub integration. The repo's `docs/` holds `technical-design/` (how the code works) and `product-design/` (what nagara is) under mahou's charter, with hand-kept indexes and relative links; that is where the detail lives. Work in flight is never in `docs/`.

**Built:** the API spine (enqueue → extract → spawn TTS → poll → audio), single API-key auth on every route, Alembic migrations, a step-based item pipeline with per-step persistence, markdown-formatted paragraphs, article images stored as image units and described with Gemini, code blocks described, a cost ledger per Firecrawl/TTS/describer call, footnote-marker pruning, XML-tagged-word and empty-element extraction fixes. The read-along player runs on tachikoma-pages, not in the repo's `web/`, which is still empty on `main`.

**Not built:** `web/`, Google OAuth, quota, settings, landing, article list. The [[mvp]] spec describes the original plan; the agreed build order is dogfood first (API hardening → article list → settings), then the public funnel (auth → article creation → landing), each in service of validating demand.

**Backlog in Linear (2026-09-07):** 40 issues on the nagara project, five milestones. **Extraction v2** (ASE-5 to ASE-10, ASE-24 to ASE-27): validation gates, recipe schema and resolver, agent recipe loop, per-recipe fetch strategy, reporting UI if still needed, the X-post bug, plus the trustworthy-extraction research, unfenced-code-as-prose, prose boilerplate and literal footnote markers. **Validate demand** (ASE-11 to ASE-13): OAuth login, web article creation, landing. **Formulas read aloud** (ASE-36 done, ASE-37 to ASE-39): MathML recovery, described display formulas, raw delimiters. **Read-along player** (ASE-40 done, ASE-41 to ASE-43): the surface, image unit rendering, playback speed. **Read-along visual design** (ASE-44). Loose: API hardening (ASE-14), article list, settings, link-and-share, single origin, describe-budget starvation, quote voice switching, audio caching, caption export, bookmarklet, three test gaps, the audible-markdown criterion, and four open questions (castable video, streaming paragraph audio, markdown faithfulness, pricing model). In Todo: ASE-5, ASE-10, ASE-24.

**Conventions:** branches are `feat/<feature-name>`; a feature is shaped and designed (mahou:shape, mahou:design) and its design lands as a note before a milestone gets implementation tasks; a spike is throwaway and never merges. The earlier LLM-in-the-hot-path extraction plan is superseded by the recipes approach and no longer exists as a record. Only `idea/read-along-player` remains as a non-main branch, kept on purpose as the player shape spike.

Turn [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]]'s existing audio-article generation into a standalone product. The pipeline already exists — chunking, TTS voice selection, audio stitching — so the bet is that the hard technical part is done and the open question is demand and packaging.

**MVP is defined** — see [[mvp]] for the full spec (surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market).

## The Idea

**Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A private personal audio read-later queue, API-first: enqueue an article (web paste or agent push) → it's generated into read-along audio → listen from your queue when it suits you. The web paste-and-listen page is the front door; the queue-for-later is the real objective, and a solid API lets [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] push reading-list items straight into it.

## Why

The pipeline is already built and working inside Tachikoma. Productizing it is mostly a matter of wrapping a demand-validation surface around code that already runs, rather than inventing the core capability.

## MVP

Full spec in [[mvp]]. In short: a private audio read-later queue with Google login, an eager `enqueue(url, voice?)` primitive shared by web and API, a 5-item/month free quota, all Kokoro voices (plus Random) with a per-user default, and an API key so Tachikoma can push items. Publicly fetchable articles only; uploads and paywalled content deferred.

## Technical Research (2026-07-10)

Ran a hands-on experiment on **Kokoro-82M** (open-weight TTS) + serverless GPU hosting. Full details in [[research]]; general reference in [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] and [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]]. Key results for this product:

- **Latency is a solved problem.** A 20-min article synthesizes in ~38 s on Replicate's T4 (zero-effort) or ~21 s on a Modal L4 — well inside a "don't leave the user waiting" budget. No exotic infra needed.
- **The pricing/token-cost open question now has real numbers:** ~**$0.008 per 20-min article** on Replicate (bills active compute only), or ~$0.004–0.005 batched on Modal. At 2,000 articles/mo that's single-digit dollars — TTS compute is **not** the cost risk it was assumed to be. A per-audio-minute usage model comfortably covers it.
- **Hosting decision: going with Modal** (Kokoro on L4 + memory snapshotting). Owned endpoint, ~6 s cold start, ~$0 at expected volume — and crucially it lets us return **timing metadata** alongside the audio, which the read-along feature needs. Design + code in [[modal-tts-service]]. (Replicate's public model was the quick validation path but doesn't return timings.)
- **Read-along is a core feature, not a bonus:** the page highlights the paragraph currently being read, synced to audio. Achieved by synthesizing paragraph-by-paragraph and tracking cumulative time for exact paragraph ranges; Kokoro's free per-word timestamps (English) are also captured for future word-level highlighting. See [[modal-tts-service]].

## Open Questions

- ~~**Pricing vs. token cost.**~~ **Largely answered** — compute is ~$0.008/20-min article; a per-audio-minute or metered-tier model works. Remaining nuance: bundling vs. metering for UX.
- **File uploads.** Handling user-provided content (PDFs, docs) is a whole surface of its own — deferred past MVP.
- **Paywalled articles.** Fetching content behind paywalls is both a technical and a legal/ethical question — deferred.
- **Is there an audience?** The entire point of starting tiny is to find out before investing. **This is now the main gate** — the tech and cost are de-risked. Validation plan (dogfood via Tachikoma, Show HN / communities, read-later + accessibility crowds) in [[mvp]]; SEO is deliberately *not* the first channel.

## Connections

- [[mvp]] — full MVP spec: surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market
- [[modal-tts-service]] — chosen hosting design + timing/highlighting approach + code
- [[research]] — TTS engine + hosting experiment, benchmarks, cost analysis
- [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] — model capabilities reference
- [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]] — hosting/cost reference
- [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] — source of the existing audio pipeline
- [[02_Areas/Daily_Notes/2026-07-05]] — original capture

**MVP is defined** — see [[mvp]] for the full spec (surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market).

## The Idea

**Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A private personal audio read-later queue, API-first: enqueue an article (web paste or agent push) → it's generated into read-along audio → listen from your queue when it suits you. The web paste-and-listen page is the front door; the queue-for-later is the real objective, and a solid API lets [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] push reading-list items straight into it.

## Why

The pipeline is already built and working inside Tachikoma. Productizing it is mostly a matter of wrapping a demand-validation surface around code that already runs, rather than inventing the core capability.

## MVP

Full spec in [[mvp]]. Turn [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]]'s existing audio-article generation into a standalone product. The pipeline already exists — chunking, TTS voice selection, audio stitching — so the bet is that the hard technical part is done and the open question is demand and packaging.

**MVP is defined** — see [[mvp]] for the full spec (surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market).

## The Idea

**Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A private personal audio read-later queue, API-first: enqueue an article (web paste or agent push) → it's generated into read-along audio → listen from your queue when it suits you. The web paste-and-listen page is the front door; the queue-for-later is the real objective, and a solid API lets [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] push reading-list items straight into it.

## Why

The pipeline is already built and working inside Tachikoma. Productizing it is mostly a matter of wrapping a demand-validation surface around code that already runs, rather than inventing the core capability.

## MVP

Full spec in [[mvp]]. In short: a private audio read-later queue with Google login, an eager `enqueue(url, voice?)` primitive shared by web and API, a 5-item/month free quota, all Kokoro voices (plus Random) with a per-user default, and an API key so Tachikoma can push items. Publicly fetchable articles only; uploads and paywalled content deferred.

## Technical Research (2026-07-10)

Ran a hands-on experiment on **Kokoro-82M** (open-weight TTS) + serverless GPU hosting. Full details in [[research]]; general reference in [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] and [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]]. Key results for this product:

- **Latency is a solved problem.** A 20-min article synthesizes in ~38 s on Replicate's T4 (zero-effort) or ~21 s on a Modal L4 — well inside a "don't leave the user waiting" budget. No exotic infra needed.
- **The pricing/token-cost open question now has real numbers:** ~**$0.008 per 20-min article** on Replicate (bills active compute only), or ~$0.004–0.005 batched on Modal. At 2,000 articles/mo that's single-digit dollars — TTS compute is **not** the cost risk it was assumed to be. A per-audio-minute usage model comfortably covers it.
- **Hosting decision: going with Modal** (Kokoro on L4 + memory snapshotting). Owned endpoint, ~6 s cold start, ~$0 at expected volume — and crucially it lets us return **timing metadata** alongside the audio, which the read-along feature needs. Design + code in [[modal-tts-service]]. (Replicate's public model was the quick validation path but doesn't return timings.)
- **Read-along is a core feature, not a bonus:** the page highlights the paragraph currently being read, synced to audio. Achieved by synthesizing paragraph-by-paragraph and tracking cumulative time for exact paragraph ranges; Kokoro's free per-word timestamps (English) are also captured for future word-level highlighting. See [[modal-tts-service]].

## Open Questions

- ~~**Pricing vs. token cost.**~~ **Largely answered** — compute is ~$0.008/20-min article; a per-audio-minute or metered-tier model works. Remaining nuance: bundling vs. metering for UX.
- **File uploads.** Handling user-provided content (PDFs, docs) is a whole surface of its own — deferred past MVP.
- **Paywalled articles.** Fetching content behind paywalls is both a technical and a legal/ethical question — deferred.
- **Is there an audience?** The entire point of starting tiny is to find out before investing. **This is now the main gate** — the tech and cost are de-risked. Validation plan (dogfood via Tachikoma, Show HN / communities, read-later + accessibility crowds) in [[mvp]]; SEO is deliberately *not* the first channel.

- **Validate demand** (ASE-11 to ASE-13): OAuth login, web article creation, landing.
- **Cloudflare migration**: move the rest of nagara next to the pipeline; what moves is not settled. Not shaped yet.
- **Recipe reconciliation**: when a domain's recipe is tested, test its older recipes too and merge variants that still match, so a multi-format domain stops flip-flopping between two recipes. Blocked on the Cloudflare migration.
- **ORM relationships**: mapped relationships instead of FK-only models, born from the production foreign-key incident (`f02f5b0`). Not shaped yet.

Loose: API hardening (ASE-14), describe-budget starvation, quote voice switching, audio caching, caption export, bookmarklet, three test gaps, the audible-markdown criterion, and four open questions (castable video, streaming paragraph audio, markdown faithfulness, pricing model).

The original v2 sketch is archived at [[04_Archive/2026-09-05-nagara-extraction-v2|extraction v2 note]].

**Name: Nagara (ながら)** — from *ながら聞き*, consuming content while doing something else.

Related: [[03_Resources/software-engineering/hegel-bend2-verified-specs]] — parked research on Hegel (property tests for the sync/extraction invariants) and Bend 2 (laws as verifiable specs for the extraction pipeline).

The repo's `docs/` holds `technical-design/` (how the code works) and `product-design/` (what nagara is) under mahou's charter, with hand-kept indexes and relative links; that is where the detail lives. Work in flight is never in `docs/`.

**Built:** the API spine (enqueue → extract → spawn TTS → poll → audio), single API-key auth on every route, Alembic migrations, a step-based item pipeline with per-step persistence, markdown-formatted paragraphs, article images stored as image units and described with Gemini, code blocks described, a cost ledger per Firecrawl/TTS/describer call. A shared recipe contract carries the markdown rules (GFM, whole lists as one unit, math swapped for its alttext, footnotes excluded). The spoken form is derived one line per block, with list item numbers and table body rows, and a unit with nothing to say is dropped. A title unit was added on 2026-09-27 and reverted the next day because it collided with the title the player already shows. The read-along player runs on tachikoma-pages, not in the repo's `web/`, which is still empty on `main`.

Turn [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]]'s existing audio-article generation into a standalone product. The pipeline already exists — chunking, TTS voice selection, audio stitching — so the bet is that the hard technical part is done and the open question is demand and packaging.

**MVP is defined** — see [[mvp]] for the full spec (surfaces, API, quota, voice, go-to-market).

## The Idea

**Pocket / Instapaper, but for audio.** A private personal audio read-later queue, API-first: enqueue an article (web paste or agent push) → it's generated into read-along audio → listen from your queue when it suits you. The web paste-and-listen page is the front door; the queue-for-later is the real objective, and a solid API lets [[01_Projects/tachikoma/README|Tachikoma]] push reading-list items straight into it.

## Why

The pipeline is already built and working inside Tachikoma. Productizing it is mostly a matter of wrapping a demand-validation surface around code that already runs, rather than inventing the core capability.

## MVP

Full spec in [[mvp]]. In short: a private audio read-later queue with Google login, an eager `enqueue(url, voice?)` primitive shared by web and API, a 5-item/month free quota, all Kokoro voices (plus Random) with a per-user default, and an API key so Tachikoma can push items. Publicly fetchable articles only; uploads and paywalled content deferred.

## Technical Research (2026-07-10)

Ran a hands-on experiment on **Kokoro-82M** (open-weight TTS) + serverless GPU hosting. Full details in [[research]]; general reference in [[03_Resources/AI/kokoro-tts|Kokoro TTS]] and [[03_Resources/AI/gpu-serverless-providers|GPU serverless providers]]. Key results for this product:

- **Latency is a solved problem.** A 20-min article synthesizes in ~38 s on Replicate's T4 (zero-effort) or ~21 s on a Modal L4 — well inside a "don't leave the user waiting" budget. No exotic infra needed.
- **The pricing/token-cost open question now has real numbers:** ~**$0.008 per 20-min article** on Replicate (bills active compute only), or ~$0.004–0.005 batched on Modal. At 2,000 articles/mo that's single-digit dollars — TTS compute is **not** the cost risk it was assumed to be. A per-audio-minute usage model comfortably covers it.
- **Hosting decision: going with Modal** (Kokoro on L4 + memory snapshotting). Owned endpoint, ~6 s cold start, ~$0 at expected volume — and crucially it lets us return **timing metadata** alongside the audio, which the read-along feature needs. Design + code in [[modal-tts-service]]. (Replicate's public model was the quick validation path but doesn't return timings.)
- **Read-along is a core feature, not a bonus:** the page highlights the paragraph currently being read, synced to audio. Achieved by synthesizing paragraph-by-paragraph and tracking cumulative time for exact paragraph ranges; Kokoro's free per-word timestamps (English) are also captured for future word-level highlighting. See [[modal-tts-service]].

## Open Questions

- ~~**Pricing vs. token cost.**~~ **Largely answered** — compute is ~$0.008/20-min article; a per-audio-minute or metered-tier model works. Remaining nuance: bundling vs. metering for UX.
- **File uploads.** Handling user-provided content (PDFs, docs) is a whole surface of its own — deferred past MVP.
- **Paywalled articles.** Fetching content behind paywalls is both a technical and a legal/ethical question — deferred.
- **Is there an audience?** The entire point of starting tiny is to find out before investing. **This is now the main gate** — the tech and cost are de-risked. Validation plan (dogfood via Tachikoma, Show HN / communities, read-later + accessibility crowds) in [[mvp]]; SEO is deliberately *not* the first channel.

# Co-authoring a Notion page with the user

Every mechanic below was run against a real page on 2026-08-13. Where something failed, the failure is written down as a limit, not a workaround.

## Your role

You and the user share one Notion page. That page is the entire interface.

The user writes. You read the page, respond inside it, and stop. You never send a chat message, never summarize the page back, never ask the user to look at something outside it. If you have something to say, it goes on the page.

You are not taking turns. You do not wait to be addressed and the user does not wait for you. You watch the page and contribute when a contribution is warranted. Most passes warrant nothing — writing nothing is a valid and frequent outcome.

Every mechanic below was run against a real page on 2026-08-13. Where something failed, the failure is written down as a limit, not a workaround.

You and the user share one Notion page. That page is the entire interface.

name: vault-sync
description: Syncs nagara's state between this repo plus its Linear project and the nagara notes in the shin-sekai Obsidian vault (../shin-sekai), in both directions. Pulls the vault, reads what changed on each side since the last sync, proposes the updates both ways, and applies only what the user approves. Use when the user asks to sync the vault, update the nagara project notes, or check the vault for new nagara ideas.
---

# Sync nagara with the shin-sekai vault

The vault at `../shin-sekai` (from the repo root: `~/workspace/asermax/shin-sekai`) holds nagara's project notes and the captures, weekly objectives and research that mention it. The repo and Linear hold what was built and what is planned. The two drift apart between syncs, and each side has things the other lacks: the vault falls behind on what shipped, and Linear misses ideas that were only captured in the vault.

The session has three steps, in order: gather, propose, apply. Nothing is written on either side before the user approves the proposal.

## 1. Gather

### The vault

Run `git pull` in the vault first; the vault's own `CLAUDE.md` requires it. Note any untracked files `git status` shows, so they are never swept into a commit later.

The nagara notes:

| Note | What it holds | What goes stale |
|---|---|---|
| `01_Projects/nagara/index.md` | The project overview. The status paragraph, `## Repo state (synced YYYY-MM-DD)` with the commit `main` was at, "Built", "Not built", the Linear backlog by milestone, and conventions | Everything above the "Turn Tachikoma's…" paragraph |
| `01_Projects/nagara/mvp.md` | The original July MVP spec | Only its top note, which links to `index#Repo state (synced YYYY-MM-DD)` |
| `02_Areas/Ideas/nagara.md` | The ideas-garden mirror: weekly objectives with their outcomes in italics, and agreed next steps | The outcome of the latest weekly objective, and the next step |
| `01_Projects/nagara/research.md`, `modal-tts-service.md`, `reference/` | The July TTS research and hosting design | Rarely; historical |
| `04_Archive/*nagara*` | Captures already processed into Linear | Never; read-only |

The last sync date is the `last-iterated` field in `index.md` and the date in its `Repo state` heading. Find everything that touched nagara since then:

- `git log --since=<last sync> --name-only` in the vault, filtered to files that mention nagara.
- `grep -rli nagara 00_Inbox 02_Areas 03_Resources 01_Projects`, then read the matching lines (`grep -n -B2 -A6`) of the files changed since the last sync. The usual sources are daily-note captures and reflections, weekly plans, inbox notes and research notes.

### The repo and Linear

- `git log --since=<last sync> --format='%h %ad %s' --date=short` on `main`, skipping `test`, `refactor` and `style` commits for the overview. Note the current `main` commit for the `Repo state` heading.
- Linear project **nagara** (team Asermax): every milestone with its progress and description, and every issue with status, milestone and labels.

## 2. Propose

Compare the two sides and propose updates in two groups.

**Vault ← repo and Linear.** Usually the larger group:

- `index.md`: the status paragraph, the `Repo state` section (commit, deployables, what was built since the last sync), and the backlog: closed milestones with what they delivered, open milestones with their issue ranges and one line each, loose issues.
- `mvp.md`: the anchor in its top note, which must match the new `Repo state` heading exactly or the link breaks.
- `Ideas/nagara.md`: the outcome of the latest weekly objective, and the next step.
- Any other link into `index.md` whose anchor carries a date.

**Linear ← vault.** Ideas, captures or research about nagara that have no Linear home yet. For each one, propose a home: an issue in an existing milestone, a loose issue, or a new milestone. Check the existing issues first, because most vault ideas already have one. Follow the work tracking rules in the repo's `CLAUDE.md`. In particular, a new milestone's description says it is to be shaped and designed before tasks are written.

Present both groups with the reason for each item, and stop. The user often excludes items. Daily-note captures, weekly plans and research notes under `03_Resources/` are the user's own records, so propose a change to them, never make one silently.

## 3. Apply

Apply only the approved items.

- **Vault edits.** Read each note before editing it. When updating `index.md`, change `last-iterated`, the `Repo state` heading date and the `mvp.md` anchor together, so the link keeps resolving. Keep the notes' existing shape: `index.md`'s sections, the italic outcome after a weekly objective.
- **Vault commit.** Stage only the files you edited, by path, never `git add .`, because the vault carries untracked folders that are not yours. Commit with `docs(nagara): sync repo state YYYY-MM-DD` and push, which is the vault's convention. Check `git log -1 --stat` to confirm every intended file is in the commit; an edit that failed silently leaves a file out.
- **Linear.** Create or move the approved milestones and issues. Linear has no done state for a milestone: it completes when all its issues are done or canceled.

End with what changed on each side, the vault commit hashes, and anything left out because the user excluded it.

Commit with `docs(nagara): sync repo state YYYY-MM-DD` and push, which is the vault's convention. Check `git log -1 --stat` to confirm every intended file is in the commit; an edit that failed silently leaves a file out.
- **Linear.** Create or move the approved milestones and issues. Linear has no done state for a milestone: it completes when all its issues are done or canceled.

Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/commit-changes

Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/commit-changes.md` if present.

# Commit changes

Commits the changes done to this repository using conventional commits (https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/). This is the one skill whose job is committing, so the user asking for it, or a skill reaching a commit step the user approved, is the consent `basics` asks for. Pushing is not part of the job.

## Message format

```
<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]
```

Types:

- **fix**: patches a bug (PATCH in semantic versioning)
- **feat**: introduces a feature (MINOR)
- A `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer marks a breaking change (MAJOR) and can go on a commit of any type. Never use the `!` after the type or scope for this.
- **build**, **chore**, **ci**, **docs**, **style**, **refactor**, **perf**, **test**, with their usual meanings from `@commitlint/config-conventional`.

Footers other than `BREAKING CHANGE: <description>` follow the git trailer format.

## Procedure

1. **Analyze the repository state.** `git status` for everything modified, added and deleted; `git diff` for the nature of each change; `git diff --staged` for anything already staged. When the project has a `CLAUDE.md` or a `.mahou/commit-changes.md` that names a scope convention or a commit convention of its own, read it and follow it.

2. **Plan the groups.** Group by logical relationship: same feature, same fix, same area. Tests, type definitions and directly related changes go with the main change. Never mix unrelated changes in one commit. Refactors go in their own commit unless small and tightly coupled to the main change.

3. **Present the groups and wait.** Always, even when there is one group and it looks obvious. Show every group with its proposed message and its file list, then ask how to proceed: with one group, proceed or split further; with several, proceed or merge. Take the user's regrouping literally.

4. **Commit each approved group.** Stage only that group's files with `git add <file>...`, then commit with the agreed message. Never `git add -A` or `git add .`; an untracked file the user did not mention is not part of any group until they say so.

   A file whose changes belong to two groups is split by hunk. The file appears under both groups with a word on which change goes where. To stage one side, write the file's diff to a temporary patch with `git diff <file> > /tmp/<name>.diff`, delete the hunks that belong to the other group while keeping the diff header, and apply it with `git apply --cached /tmp/<name>.diff`. Once that group is committed, the hunks left in the working tree are what `git add <file>` stages for the other. `git add -p` is interactive and does not run here.

## Message rules

- Description in the imperative, present tense: "add", not "added" or "adding". Short, no trailing period.
- The message says **what** the change does, never why it was made or where the request came from. "fix(auth): add null check for expired tokens", never "fix: address PR comments".
- A body, when needed, is simple and direct: no file listings, no implementation walkthrough, no test section.
- **Scope** is the area of the project the change touches: the top-level module, directory, package or service name, one or two lowercase words. Check `git log` for the scopes the project already uses and reuse them. When the change spans areas, use the primary one; when nothing dominates, omit the scope.

## When something is off

- No changes: say so and stop.
- Merge conflict markers in the tree: say so and stop; nothing is committed over a conflict.
- Untracked files: ask whether they belong in a group before staging them.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/agus/workspace/asermax/claude-plugins/mahou/skills/basics

# Mahou

The agent is the magic: tireless, fast, and exactly as wise as the instructions it is given. The user is the spellcaster. They draw the circle, they provide the mana, they choose the spell, and the agent pours itself into the shape they drew.

No spell casts itself. No skill picks a library, no skill chooses between two designs, no skill guesses what the user meant. The agent brings facts and state; every fork comes back to the spellcaster as a question.

Skills stay small enough that the user can see what each one did and correct it, instead of large enough that they have to trust the outcome.

## Philosophy

Each skill does one job; when a skill needs a second job, it becomes two skills. A skill tells you how to work, while facts about technologies and tools live in the wiki. Nothing is committed unprompted; when work is ready, say so and wait.

## Rules

1. Never use the phrase "load-bearing".
2. **Never decide for the user.** Map the state, then ask. No recommendations, no leaning toward an option, no answering for them. Give a recommendation only when the user asks for one. mahou:program-design is the one exception: it proposes the details of a design whose decisions are already settled, grounded in the code and the conventions, and the user corrects each proposal.
3. **Report what you found, not what you assume.** When something is missing, say it is missing. Do not fill the gap with a plausible guess.
4. **Never commit or push as a side effect.** A skill whose entire job is committing, invoked directly by the user, is the exception, because that invocation is the consent.
5. **One job.** If the work in front of you has grown a second job, stop and say so rather than quietly doing both.
6. **Never volunteer next steps.** Answer what was asked, then stop. Do not close a report with work the user did not request: no "still outstanding", no "you may also want to", no queue of follow-ups. If something blocks the job in front of you, state it in one line as a fact. Everything else waits until they ask.

## Code

Comments never go inside a structure definition. Object and array literals, payloads, config entries, test fixtures, interface and type property lists, props, parameter lists: a reader scans all of these as a shape, and a comment between two entries breaks the scan. When the rationale is real, it goes above the structure or at the site that consumes the value.

This holds in every repository, whatever the language.

## Scratch folder

Every artifact a skill produces for the user and keeps between rounds goes under `.scratch/<change-slug>/` in the project's root, never under `/tmp`: a design handoff, a prototype, a draft, a research file. One directory named after the current change, holding the files the skill writes: `handoff.md`, `design.md`, `research.md`, a `prototypes/` folder, a `reports/` folder, a `test-design/` folder, a `spikes/` folder, whatever the skill defines. A skill that reopens a file reopens it from there, so the folder survives compaction, restarts and the next day. Throwaway files that are not to be reused, such as a diagram written only to validate it, may still use `/tmp`.

Skills say "the change's scratch folder" and name only the path inside it.

## The wiki

Knowledge about technologies and tools, their gotchas and their patterns, lives in mahou:wiki, indexed one level per folder so entries load on demand. Load it now and read its root indexes, global and local, so that you know which topics have entries when they come up in conversation. Read an entry only when the skill you are running says so, or when the user asks for a check against the conventions for a technology. Do not bring an entry's conventions into a question the user has not asked; when a topic with an entry comes up in a decision, say the entry exists and offer to read it.

The wiki is the standard the conventions reviewer measures a change against. mahou:learn writes it.

## The project's docs

Projects mahou runs in keep their own documentation in a folder they own, usually `docs/`. How to find it and what its structure is made of live in mahou:docs, which every skill and agent that reads or writes documentation loads. Skills that do not touch documentation leave it alone.

## The local layer

A project can change how a skill behaves in a `.mahou/` folder at its root: `.mahou/basics.md` for standing rules, `.mahou/<skill>.md` for one skill, `.mahou/wiki/` for local knowledge. Every skill reads its own file when present, and local wins over global when the two conflict.

## Reporting to the user

When a skill hands the user a report, such as findings, an investigation's answer, or a summary of a change, it loads mahou:report. That skill carries the shape a report should take: what comes first, when to diagram, how to separate fact from claim, and the unslop rules to hold while writing it.
